quote.translation: In spite of his emphasis on "judgement", consequently, and in spite of his rejection of "gamblers", he acknowledges that at least one half of "the charm of horse racing" still lies in the play of chance, in "winning and losing by chance" .

regions.text: することを認めてゐるものである。

quote.translation: What, then, is the character of the chance immanent in horse racing?

regions.text: ・然らば競馬に内在する偶然とは如何なる性格のものであらうか。姿ころの場合と同様に、徹視偶然は巨視地平に於てのみ成立するものとして、徹視的地平にあつては馬の者順はすべて因果約決定を有つてゐると云へるでもあらう。

quote.translation: As in the case of the die, we might take microscopic chance to be something that holds only on the macroscopic horizon, and so say that on the microscopic horizon the order in which the horses finish is causally determined throughout.

regions.text: さうすれば、實際問題としての偶然性は認識の不十全性に依存する主觀のものに解滑してしまふであらう。

quote.translation: Contingency as a practical problem would then dissolve into something subjective, dependent on the incompleteness of our knowledge.

regions.text: さういふ偶然性は親客の認識程度に應じて主親的に度合を異にするものであり心的機構全礎と開聯して偶然性の心理的研究の對象を構成するだけのものである。

quote.translation: Contingency of that kind differs in degree, subjectively, according to how much the spectators know, and it merely constitutes, in connection with the whole mental mechanism, the object of a psychological study of contingency.

regions.text: しかもなほ、さういふ主親偶然とは獨立して、哲學には客親な偶然性が存してるる。

quote.translation: And yet, independently of such subjective chance, there exists, philosophically, an objective contingency.

regions.text: A馬が一着を占めたときに、A馬の一着は必すしも絕對必然性を有つてはゐない。A馬が二着であり三者である場合を考へることが論理約に矛盾を含まない限りA馬一者の事實に偶然性が存するのである。

quote.translation: When horse A has taken first place, horse A's first place does not necessarily possess absolute necessity, and so long as it involves no logical contradiction to think of the case in which horse A came second or third, contingency lies in the fact of horse A's first place.

regions.text: 因果決定があらゆる細目に於て存し、且つそれが假りに悉く認識されてゐたとすれば、豫め着願も悉く認識されてあるわけであるからその場合は競馬は時間的鰹過としては成立しないであらう。

quote.translation: If causal determination existed in every detail, and if, let us suppose, it were all known, then the order of finishing would also be known entirely in advance, and in that case horse racing would presumably not take place as a course in time.
